newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds fall on US jobs data, domestic worries.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds fall on US jobs data, domestic worries.

text.p: Irish bonds slumped in moderate selling on Friday on the back of mixed U.S. jobs data and a variety of domestic worries, dealers said.

"The U.S. non-farm payroll figures have knocked things back today generally but the domestic climate is by no means supportive," a dealer said. "Yesterday's banking statistics unsettled the market, the punt is under pressure, and there are worries about today's election resulting in a hung parliament."
The Irish yield curve had flattened considerably, dealers said, with the short end underperforming sharply against Germany.
By 1515 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 25 pence at 101.45 to yield 6.10 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 25 pence at 108.55 to yield 6.71 percent.
Dealers said yields against German bunds stood at 168 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 90 over in the 10-year.
While U.S. data on Friday showed a below-forecast 138,000 rise in US non-farm payrolls in May, the April figure was revised up to 323,000 from an initial 142,000.
Meanwhile, acceleration in Ireland's private sector credit in Thursday's banking statistics spooked the market, with the year-on-year rate rising to 19 percent in April from 18.6 percent in March.
The data had triggered selling at the short end, dealers said.
Also, pressure on the Irish pound continues to generate fears that a near term interest rate rise is on the cards.
The Bank of England's hike in official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent on Friday had already been priced in, Irish dealers said.

Worries that Friday's election could result in a market-unfriendly hung parliament had prompted net selling by both domestic and foreign investors during the week, dealers said, although latest polls suggest the opposition Fianna Fail-Progressive Democrat alliance will win a majority.
Worries about the prospects for EMU going ahead on time were also spooking the market, dealers said.
